title: IB Language Acquisition Individual Oral Prep…
summary: Build a realistic September-November IB Language Acquisition Individual Oral prep timeline for HL extracts, analysis, speaking, and timed practice.
body_markdown:
If your IB Language Acquisition individual oral will take place in November or early winter, begin structured preparation in **September** . You do not need intensive daily rehearsals three months in advance, but you need enough time to strengthen vocabulary, analysis, and spontaneous speaking.


For **Language B HL** , this means reviewing both literary works and practising with varied passages without trying to predict the official extracts. For **Language B SL and language ab initio** , the opening presentation uses a visual stimulus, so preparation should focus on interpreting unfamiliar images. This **IB Language Acquisition Individual Oral prep timeline** covers September to November, with particular attention to HL extract analysis.


### First, confirm which Language Acquisition oral you are taking


The Diploma Programme Language Acquisition group includes **Language B** and **language ab initio** , but their oral tasks differ. The official IB pages for[Language B](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/language-acquisition/language-b/) and[language ab initio](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/language-acquisition/language-ab-initio/) explain the distinction.


Course Opening stimulus What to prepare


**Language B HL** An unseen extract from one of the two literary works studied Whole-work knowledge, passage analysis, literary vocabulary, discussion skills


**Language B SL** An unseen visual stimulus connected to a prescribed theme Description, interpretation, cultural connections, thematic vocabulary


**Language ab initio** An unseen visual stimulus connected to a prescribed theme Clear description, personal response, cultural awareness, accessible spontaneous language


Under the current Language B structure, the individual oral is worth **25%** of the final subject grade. At HL, students receive two extracts, one from each studied literary work, and select one. Extracts are up to approximately **300 words** , with **20 minutes** of supervised preparation.


The oral lasts **12-15 minutes** . It includes a **3-4 minute presentation** , a **4-5 minute follow-up discussion** , and a **5-6 minute general discussion** beginning from one or more course themes. The official[IB Language B subject brief](https://ibo.org/contentassets/5895a05412144fe890312bad52b17044/lang-b-2018-en.pdf) confirms the weighting and different SL and HL stimuli. The IB's[assessment comparison appendix](https://ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/university-admission/pdfs/ecctis_ib-dp-cefr_appendices_august_2023.pdf) provides the detailed structure.


Your school determines the assessment date within the permitted schedule. There is no universal IB rule requiring completion in November, so confirm your date with your teacher.


### An important rule about preparing HL extracts


At Language B HL, **your teacher selects the official extracts** , and you must not know beforehand which passages will appear. Preparing extracts means practising with varied important passages, not memorizing the passage you expect to receive.


A useful passage bank can include turning points, conflicts, revealing conversations, perspective shifts, and moments connected to major ideas. Practise a repeatable analytical process rather than writing polished speeches.


For each practice passage, ask:


1. **Context:** Where does this moment occur?
2. **Content:** What is happening, and which conflict or idea develops?
3. **Character:** What do words, actions, or relationships reveal?
4. **Craft:** Which language or structural choices shape meaning?
5. **Connection:** How does the passage relate to the wider work, target-language culture, or an IB theme?


RevisionDojo's guide to the[Language B HL literary oral](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-language-b-hl-individual-oral-literature) explains why the task requires supported interpretation but should not become a Language A-style commentary.


### September: build knowledge before increasing pressure


September should establish your foundations. For a November oral, aim for **three short sessions each week** , totaling approximately 90-120 minutes.


### Weeks 1-2: map both literary works


Create a one-page overview for each HL work. Include:


- title, author, genre, and relevant cultural context
- main characters and relationships
- major turning points and central ideas
- recurring symbols or stylistic patterns
- links to **identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organization,** and **sharing the planet**


This is more useful than detailed chapter summaries that are difficult to retrieve quickly. You need to place an unseen extract within the complete work and explain its significance. Review the[Language B literature requirement](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-language-b-literature-requirement) if you are unsure about the two HL works.


### Weeks 3-4: build usable language


Create vocabulary clusters for character, conflict, tone, change, context, and interpretation. Learn target-language phrases equivalent to “this reveals,” “the contrast suggests,” and “this moment marks a change.”


Do not memorize isolated technical terms. Use each phrase in a complete spoken sentence, then turn recurring errors and useful expressions into Flashcards. The[Language B revision guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-language-acquisition-how-to-effectively-revise-for-language-b-exams) explains how to learn reusable language rather than disconnected lists.


By the end of September, record one untimed **3-4 minute** analysis from each work. Listen for excessive summary, repeated vocabulary, unclear organization, and unsupported claims.


### October: move from knowledge to performance


October is the main development month. Increase to **three or four sessions per week** , keeping most sessions between 20 and 35 minutes.


Week Main task Evidence of progress


**Week 1** Analyse two passages, one from each work Each response includes context, two developed observations, and support


**Week 2** Add follow-up questions Answers include reasons, explanations, or examples


**Week 3** Practise general thematic discussion You can discuss all five themes without a script


**Week 4** Complete two full simulations You remain within time and recover naturally from mistakes


Use this speaking pattern: **observation, evidence, interpretation, significance** . Identify a detail, refer to wording in the passage, explain what it reveals, and connect it to the wider conflict or work.


Include at least one unpredictable conversation each week. Ask a partner, teacher, tutor, or Jojo AI to challenge an interpretation, request clarification, or move to a cultural issue. A memorized presentation cannot compensate for weak interaction later in the oral.


The[RevisionDojo oral practice guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/mastering-language-b-oral-practice) outlines a record, review, and re-record cycle. The[Language B speaking guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-improve-your-language-b-speaking-skills-proven-strategies-and-revisiondojo-tips) also covers pronunciation, repair phrases, and spontaneous expansion.


### November: simulate the assessment, then reduce the workload


During early November, practise under realistic conditions. Select two unfamiliar passages, allow **20 minutes** to choose and prepare one, and deliver the presentation without restarting. Continue with follow-up questions and a general thematic discussion.


Complete no more than **two full simulations per week** . On other days, use short drills for weaknesses identified in recordings, such as inaccurate tenses, vague textual references, unclear pronunciation, or brief answers.


In the final five to seven days:


- review your one-page maps of both works
- rehearse flexible openings and transitions
- answer short questions across all five themes
- complete one final simulation early in the week
- avoid learning a new speech or large vocabulary list
- confirm the time, location, and permitted materials


Final preparation should make you adaptable, not over-rehearsed. The night before, brief review and normal sleep are more useful than repeatedly recording the same response.


### Common preparation mistakes


**Trying to predict the official extract** is unreliable and may produce a rehearsed response that fails to address the passage. Prepare both works evenly.


**Retelling the plot** also weakens analysis. Give enough context to orient the listener, then explain ideas, relationships, language, and significance.


**Ignoring the conversation sections** limits performance because communication and interaction are assessed beyond the presentation. Practise clarifying, justifying, and extending answers.


Do not confuse this with the Language A individual oral. Language B HL uses one unseen extract chosen from two teacher-selected options and does not require a student-selected global issue or comparison of two extracts.


### Conclusion


For a November assessment, effective **fall oral prep Language Acquisition** begins in September with knowledge and vocabulary, develops analysis and interaction in October, and shifts to simulations in November. HL students should practise many passages while remembering that official extracts remain unseen. SL and ab initio students can follow the same schedule using unfamiliar visual stimuli.
